name: Sofwave SUPERB

lead: Sofwave is a non-invasive aesthetic device that uses its SUPERB (Synchronous Ultrasound Parallel BEam) technology to deliver ultrasound energy into the middle layer of the skin. The company describes it as FDA-cleared for lifting the eyebrows, the neck and the area under the chin, and for improving the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles.

The aim is firmer, lifted-looking skin without surgery or needles. Ultrasound heats the mid-dermis, which the company says prompts the skin to produce more collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid over the following weeks.

paras: A clinician moves the handpiece over the treatment area in a single session. The company describes minimal downtime, with patients able to resume makeup, exercise and normal activity afterwards. Results are said to build over weeks as the skin responds.

The manufacturer describes the treatment as safe for all skin types and with minimal downtime. Published studies of parallel-beam ultrasound report on efficacy and safety, and as with energy-based devices, heat-related effects such as redness or discomfort are possible. Anyone considering it would discuss suitability with a clinician.

chain: Skin remodelling raises collagen and elastin
Firmer, lifted-looking skin on brow, neck and jawline
angle.text: Clients choose it for non-surgical lifting of the brow and under-chin area and for softer-looking lines.

lead: Sofwave is a needle-free, ultrasound-based face and body treatment aimed at firmer, lifted-looking skin. Its technology, branded SUPERB (Synchronous Ultrasound Parallel BEam), uses parallel ultrasound beams that pass through the skin surface and heat tissue in the mid-dermis, the layer that gives skin much of its firmness.[1] People choose it to lift the brow, neck and under-chin area, soften fine lines and wrinkles and, in newer indications, improve acne scars and the look of cellulite.[1]

The company lists US FDA clearances for lifting the eyebrows, neck and submental area, improving the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles, acne scars and the short-term appearance of cellulite. It says the heat stimulates production of collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid and that there is no downtime.[1]

Clinical papers on high-intensity, high-frequency, non-focused parallel-beam ultrasound have been published in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology, covering skin tightening, facial skin laxity, acne scars and cellulite, mostly in small prospective or retrospective studies.
infobox: Brow, neck and submental lift; fine lines and wrinkles; acne scars; short-term cellulite appearance[1]
Pure Impact, a muscle-stimulation body treatment[1]

paras: Sofwave positions itself as a regenerative aesthetics company and describes its device as non-invasive and needle-free. A clinician applies a handpiece to the skin and the ultrasound is delivered to the mid-dermal layer without surface injury, which the company presents as the reason the treatment suits all skin types and colours, including darker skin that is described as more vulnerable to burns.[1] The company says patients can resume makeup, workouts and normal activity right afterwards.[1]

The manufacturer says ultrasound passes through the skin surface to heat mid-dermal tissue, triggering a regenerative response that produces collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid.[1] Peer-reviewed papers describe related devices as high-intensity, high-frequency, non-focused ultrasound parallel beams, in contrast to focused ultrasound systems that concentrate energy at points. A pathology-based paper on parallel ultrasound facial tightening, published in 2025, and a 2025 Dermatologic Surgery paper on long-term extracellular matrix remodelling have also appeared in the literature.[2]

The company lists lifting of the eyebrows, the neck and the area under the chin, improvement of fine lines and wrinkles, acne scars and the short-term appearance of cellulite.[1] Studies of the technology have looked at nasolabial folds and marionette lines, lax skin of the brow, under-chin and neck, facial acne scars and cellulite of the thighs and buttocks.

Sofwave also markets Pure Impact, a separate whole-body bio-electrical muscle stimulation device cleared for strengthening, toning and firming the abdomen, buttocks, thighs and arms, which the company says emulates plyometric exercise.[1]

Treatment is delivered by a clinician in an office visit with a handheld applicator. The studies describe one to two sessions: the facial laxity trial used two treatment sessions with follow-up at 3 and 6 months, the acne scar study used a single treatment, and the cellulite study used two sessions with follow-up to 3 months. Patients rated discomfort immediately afterwards, with reported mean pain scores of 3.94 to 6.64 on 0-10 scales. Results are described as building over weeks as the skin responds; in one study improvement in nasolabial folds and marionette lines was seen at 1 month and was stable at 3 months.

A study led by Hongcharu, Boonchoo and Gold in 2023 evaluated a parallel-beam device with a 1.5 mm treatment depth for skin tightening. Thirty-six participants were photographed and scanned with Antera 3D imaging at baseline, 1 month and 3 months; depression volumes of the nasolabial folds and marionette lines fell significantly at 1 and 3 months, with no significant change between the two follow-ups, a reduction in more than 60 percent of participants as early as 1 month, a mean pain score of 6.64, and no adverse events reported.

In a 2024 prospective trial by Gold and Biron, 15 subjects aged 40 to 69 had two treatments for lax skin of the eyebrow, submental and neck areas and were assessed at 3 and 6 months with physician global aesthetic improvement scoring. An improvement pattern was seen in all treated areas and remained stable; mean pain was 5.6, and the authors described the improvement as safe with tolerable pain.

A 2025 retrospective preliminary study by Boonchoo and Hongcharu treated 14 Thai adults with facial acne scars using a single session. A blinded dermatologist scored photos, and scar volume measured with Antera 3D improved significantly across follow-up to 8 months; mean pain was 3.94 and no adverse events were reported.

A 2025 multicentre, open-label, non-randomized study by Gold and colleagues treated the thighs and buttocks of 60 adults aged 23 to 65 with a high-density handpiece for cellulite, in two sessions. Three blinded physicians scored improvement on the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale in 91 percent of treated areas, a 69 percent improvement on the Cellulite Severity Scale, 53 percent on the Laxity Scale and satisfaction in 73 percent of subjects; mean pain was 4.26 and no serious adverse events were reported.

Further parallel-ultrasound papers include a 2025 clinical and pathologic study of facial tightening, a 2026 study of skin laxity and wrinkles in Asian patients in Lasers in Surgery and Medicine, and a 2026 report on melasma in Asian skin.[2] Most studies are small, and several are single-arm, open-label or retrospective.[2]

The company site describes the treatment as clinically proven, safe, quick and natural-looking, and lists awards including the 2025 Shape Beauty Award, the 2025 UK Women's Health Skincare Award, New Beauty Magazine awards in 2022 to 2024, a Good Housekeeping 2023 Best Anti-Aging Pro Treatment award, a Cosmopolitan 2022 Holy Grail Beauty Award and the ELLE Future of Beauty Award in 2021.[1] The page does not include study data, so these are company statements.

The manufacturer describes the treatment as safe for all skin types with minimal downtime.[1] The published studies above reported no adverse events in the 36-participant and 14-participant studies and no serious adverse events in the 60-participant cellulite study, while all reported treatment discomfort of moderate level on pain scales. As with other energy-based devices, heat-related effects are the category's main concern, and suitability is assessed by a clinician. The device is listed by the company as FDA-cleared for its indications; clearance dates are not given on the page.[1]

lore.intro: Sofwave is a clinic-delivered branded device, so most claims come from the company and from clinicians publishing small studies.
